title: How Writing is marked: the four criteria
what: Your Writing is marked on four things. Each one is worth 25% of your score, so no single one can be ignored. Task 2 is worth twice as much as Task 1, so it deserves more of your time. 'Criteria' just means the things the examiner looks for.

steps.do: Task Achievement (Task 1) or Task Response (Task 2): answer every part of the question, with a clear overview or a clear opinion.
steps.why: If you miss part of the task, your score for this criterion is limited, however good your English is.

steps.do: Coherence and Cohesion: put one main idea in each paragraph, and link your sentences so the reader never gets lost.
steps.why: Examiners read fast. Clear paragraphs and links make your answer easy to follow, which earns marks.

steps.do: Lexical Resource: use a range of precise words, and use them correctly. Avoid repeating the same word many times.
steps.why: Vocabulary is the words you know. Examiners reward the right word more than a big word used wrongly.

steps.do: Grammatical Range and Accuracy: mix simple and complex sentences, and keep most of them error-free.
steps.why: Grammar is judged on two things: how varied it is, and how correct it is. You need both.

steps.do: Spend more time on Task 2. Aim for about 40 minutes on it and 20 on Task 1.
steps.why: Task 2 counts double. A weak essay costs you twice as many marks as a weak report.

steps.do: Aim for the next band, not perfection. Pick one habit from the Band 6 to 7 list below and practise it.
steps.why: Small, specific habits raise your score faster than trying to improve everything at once.

steps.do: Read your practice answers as an examiner. Score each of the four criteria separately, from the checklist.
steps.why: Knowing which criterion is weakest tells you exactly what to practise next.

tricks: Band 6 to 7, Task Achievement: at Band 6 you cover the task but some points are unclear or too long. At Band 7 you give a clear overview or position and pick the key points.
Band 6 to 7, Coherence: at Band 6 you use linking words, but sometimes too many or too few. At Band 7 each paragraph has one clear topic and the links feel natural.
Band 6 to 7, Vocabulary: at Band 6 you use enough words but repeat some and make some spelling mistakes. At Band 7 you choose precise words and make only a few small slips.

Band 6 to 7, Grammar: at Band 6 you use some complex sentences, but errors are noticeable, though they rarely stop the reader understanding. At Band 7 you use many complex sentences and most are correct.
traps: Thinking long words win marks. A simple word used correctly beats a difficult word used wrongly. Use the word you are sure about.
Writing under the minimum word count. Task 1 needs 150 words and Task 2 needs 250. Fewer words limits your score, so reach the minimum.
Memorising a whole answer. Examiners notice memorised text and it can lower your score. Learn useful phrases and frames, not full paragraphs.
Ignoring a part of the question. If the question has two parts, answer both. Check the question again before you finish.
checklist: Did I answer every part of the question?
Does each paragraph have one clear main idea?
Did I avoid repeating the same word again and again?
Did I use some complex sentences, and did I check them for errors?

demo.prompt: Score this short Task 2 paragraph on the four criteria, one at a time. Then improve the two weakest criteria. Question: 'Some people think cars should be banned from city centres. Do you agree?' Paragraph: 'Many people think cars are bad for cities. I agree because the air is dirty and there is a lot of traffic. Cars is causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.'

moves.say: I start with Task Achievement. The paragraph says 'I agree' clearly, so it answers the question. I give it about Band 6.
moves.build: Many people think cars are bad for cities. I agree because the air is dirty and there is a lot of traffic. Cars is causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: Next, Coherence and Cohesion. Each sentence follows the one before, and the reasons come straight after my view. I give it about Band 6.
moves.build: Many people think cars are bad for cities. I agree because the air is dirty and there is a lot of traffic. Cars is causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: Now Lexical Resource. 'Bad' and 'dirty' are correct but vague. I give it about Band 5, so I will improve it.
moves.build: Many people think cars are bad for cities. I agree because the air is dirty and there is a lot of traffic. Cars is causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: I swap 'bad' for 'harmful' and 'dirty' for 'polluted'. Both words are more precise, and the meaning stays the same.
moves.build: Many people think cars are harmful to cities. I agree because the air is polluted and there is a lot of traffic. Cars is causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: Grammar has a clear error: 'Cars is causing'. 'Cars' is plural, so I change 'is' to 'are'. Nothing else needs changing.
moves.build: Many people think cars are harmful to cities. I agree because the air is polluted and there is a lot of traffic. Cars are causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: I give Task 2 about 40 minutes and Task 1 about 20, so Task 2 gets the extra time.
moves.build: Many people think cars are harmful to cities. I agree because the air is polluted and there is a lot of traffic. Cars are causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: To reach Band 7, I keep swapping vague words for precise ones. 'A lot of traffic' becomes 'heavy congestion', which is more exact.
moves.build: Many people think cars are harmful to cities. I agree because the air is polluted and there is heavy congestion. Cars are causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

moves.say: I score each criterion on its own, not as one mark. Task Achievement and Coherence are about Band 6 here, so I note both.
moves.build: Many people think cars are harmful to cities. I agree because the air is polluted and there is heavy congestion. Cars are causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

demo.answer: Many people think cars are harmful to cities. I agree because the air is polluted and there is heavy congestion. Cars are causing many problems. Governments should do something about it.

band8.band8: Covers every part of the task and states a clear overview (Task 1) or a clear position (Task 2) that the whole answer supports.

band8.typical: Uses linking words like "firstly" and "also" in every sentence, so the text feels mechanical.
band8.band8: Gives each paragraph one clear idea, and links sentences with reference words and natural connectors, not a connector in every line.

band8.band8: Uses a range of precise words and collocations, paraphrases the question, and makes only rare small slips.

band8.typical: Writes mostly simple sentences, or tries complex ones with frequent errors.
band8.band8: Mixes simple and complex sentences on purpose, and most sentences have no errors at all.

band8.typical: Spends equal time on both tasks, so Task 2 stays short and thin.
band8.band8: Remembers Task 2 counts twice as much as Task 1, so gives it about 40 minutes and a fully developed answer.

title: Timing and planning: 60 minutes, two tasks
what: You have 60 minutes for two tasks, and there is no extra time. Good timing is a skill you can practise. A short plan before you write makes the answer clearer and saves time later.

steps.do: Start with Task 1. Spend about 20 minutes on it: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check.
steps.why: Task 1 is shorter and easier to finish. Doing it first gives you a safe start and leaves a clear 40 minutes for Task 2.

steps.do: Move to Task 2 at the 20-minute mark. Spend 5 to plan, 30 to write and 5 to check.
steps.why: Task 2 counts double, so it needs the bigger share of the time. Stick to the clock.

steps.do: In the plan, write short notes only: your overview or position, and one main idea for each paragraph.
steps.why: A plan is for you, not the examiner. Keep it short so you have time to write.

steps.do: Write at least 150 words for Task 1 and 250 words for Task 2. Count words in your practice, not in the real test.
steps.why: Below the minimum, your score is limited. Counting in practice teaches you how long your writing is.

steps.do: Do not pad. Cut sentences that repeat an idea or add nothing, and write only what answers the question.
steps.why: Padding wastes time and can lower coherence. A clear 170-word report beats a messy 220-word one.

steps.do: Keep the last minutes of each task for the grammar checklist in the 'Grammar fixes' note.
steps.why: Most small errors can be found in two minutes. These are the cheapest marks you will earn.

steps.do: If you run out of time, write a short ending or overview and stop. Do not leave the answer unfinished.
steps.why: An answer with no conclusion or overview loses marks for the task. A simple ending is better than none.

tricks: Practise with a timer. Writing Task 1 in 20 minutes feels fast at first, but it gets easier after a few tries.
Plan on your scratch paper, in the margin. Use two or three words per idea, not full sentences.
Write your overview in the plan stage. For Task 1 this is the most important sentence, so decide it before you start the body.
Check the clock at set times: 20 minutes for the end of Task 1, 55 minutes for starting your final check.
traps: Spending 30 minutes on Task 1 because it is first. Task 2 is worth more, so protect its time.
Skipping the plan to save time. Without a plan you often repeat yourself or forget the overview, and then lose more time.
Counting every word while writing. It wastes time. Type on screen and watch the on-screen word count instead. If you take Writing on Paper, count lines in your handwriting.
Rewriting a whole paragraph in the check stage. Fix small errors instead, because there is no time for big changes.
checklist: Do I know my time for each task: 5, 12, 3 and 5, 30, 5?
Did I start with Task 1 and leave 40 minutes for Task 2?
Did I plan my overview or position before writing?
Do I have 2 or 3 minutes left for the grammar checklist?

demo.prompt: You have 5 minutes to plan a Task 1 answer. Task 1 needs at least 150 words. The bar chart shows visitors to a museum, in thousands, for adults and children in 2019 and 2020. Adults: 120 in 2019, 80 in 2020. Children: 60 in 2019, 90 in 2020.

moves.build: Time: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check.

moves.say: At the 20-minute mark I move to Task 2: 5 to plan, 30 to write and 5 to check.
moves.build: Time: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check.

moves.say: I pick my key features and write them as short notes, not sentences. Adults fell and children rose, which are the two big stories.
moves.build: Time: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check. Key features: adults fell from 120 to 80; children rose from 60 to 90.

moves.say: Next I choose my overview. It is the big picture with no numbers, so I note the two trends in plain words.
moves.build: Time: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check. Key features: adults fell from 120 to 80; children rose from 60 to 90. Overview: adults down, children up, no numbers.

moves.say: I note my word target at the top, so I know how much to write. Task 1 needs at least 150 words, and I will count in practice.

moves.build: Time: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check. Key features: adults fell from 120 to 80; children rose from 60 to 90. Overview: adults down, children up, no numbers. Target: at least 150 words.

moves.say: If time runs out, I write a short ending or overview and stop, so the answer is never left unfinished.
moves.build: Time: 5 to plan, 12 to write, 3 to check. Key features: adults fell from 120 to 80; children rose from 60 to 90. Overview: adults down, children up, no numbers. Target: at least 150 words.

band8.typical: Starts Task 1 without a plan and notices the missing overview in the last minute.
band8.band8: Spends 5 minutes choosing the overview and the key figures, then writes them down as short notes before starting.

band8.typical: Uses 30 minutes on Task 1, then rushes Task 2, which counts twice as much.
band8.band8: Stops Task 1 at 20 minutes and gives Task 2 the full 40, with a short position and two ideas planned first.

band8.typical: Plans nothing, so ideas repeat or arrive in a random order across paragraphs.
band8.band8: Notes one main idea per paragraph in the plan, so each paragraph has its own job and the order is already clear.

band8.typical: Spends the last minutes rereading without looking for specific problems.
band8.band8: Uses the last minutes to hunt for repeated words and swap one or two for precise alternatives.

band8.typical: Skips the final check, so careless errors in articles and verbs stay in the answer.
band8.band8: Keeps 2 to 3 minutes per task to scan for articles, verb forms and plurals, and fixes small errors only.

title: Grammar fixes: the eight most common errors
what: Small grammar mistakes are the most common reason for lost marks, and they are easy to fix when you know what to look for. Use this note as your checking list in the last minutes of each task. Each fix has a wrong sentence and a right one.

steps.do: Articles: use 'a' or 'an' for one general thing and 'the' for something specific. Wrong: 'Number of cars rose.' Right: 'The number of cars rose.'
steps.why: Articles are small words that are easy to forget. Missing them is one of the most common errors.

steps.do: Subject-verb agreement: match the verb to the subject. Wrong: 'The price of oil rise.' Right: 'The price of oil rises.'
steps.why: With he, she, it or one thing, the present verb ends in -s. Check the real subject, not the word nearest the verb.

steps.do: Tense for dates: use past tense for past years. Wrong: 'In 2010 sales are 50.' Right: 'In 2010 sales were 50.'
steps.why: The date tells you the tense. A past year needs past tense, and a future year needs 'will' or 'is expected to'.

steps.do: Comma splice: do not join two sentences with only a comma. Wrong: 'Sales rose, profits fell.' Right: 'Sales rose, but profits fell.'
steps.why: A comma is not strong enough to join two full sentences. Use a full stop, 'but', 'while' or 'and'.

steps.do: There is or there are: match to what follows. Wrong: 'There is many reasons.' Right: 'There are many reasons.'
steps.why: Look at the noun after the verb. One thing uses 'is', and more than one uses 'are'.

steps.do: Plural -s: add -s after numbers and words like 'many'. Wrong: 'Three million tourist visited.' Right: 'Three million tourists visited.'
steps.why: A missing -s tells the examiner you do not control plurals. Check every noun after a number.

steps.do: Spell words from the prompt correctly. Wrong: 'goverment'. Right: 'government'. Copy them letter by letter from the question on screen.
steps.why: The prompt words are given to you. A mistake there looks careless and costs vocabulary marks.

steps.do: Use 'the number of' for countable things. Wrong: 'The amount of cars rose.' Right: 'The number of cars rose.'
steps.why: Cars, people and jobs can be counted. Water, money and traffic cannot be counted, so they use 'the amount of'.

tricks: Read your answer once for each error type. Look for only articles first, then only verbs, then only plurals.
Check each verb by asking 'when?'. If the time is past, the verb should be past.
If a long sentence has a comma and no joining word, split it into two sentences. Short and correct is better than long and wrong.
Learn your own top two errors. Write them on a card and check for them first in every practice answer.
traps: Trying new complex grammar in the last minute. Fix what you can see is wrong instead of making risky changes.
Relying on a spell checker. There is none in the test, so practise by hand and note the words you misspell.
Changing a correct sentence into a wrong one. Only change a sentence when you know the rule.
Ignoring one-word endings. Missing -s, -ed and -ing is the most common mistake, and it is easy to miss when reading fast.
checklist: Does every singular countable noun have a, an, the or another word before it?
Do my verbs match their subjects, and match the time (past, present or future)?
Is every comma between two full sentences joined by a linking word?
Did I check plurals and the spelling of words copied from the question?

demo.prompt: Correct this learner sentence, one error at a time. The town has only one museum. It has three errors: 'In 2010 the number of tourist visiting museum rise.'

moves.say: I read the sentence and spot three errors. I fix one at a time, starting with the article, because articles are easy to miss.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourist visiting museum rise.

moves.say: 'The museum' means the only museum in town, so it needs 'the'. I add 'the' and change nothing else.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourist visiting the museum rise.

moves.say: Next, agreement. 'The number' is singular, so its verb must match it. I hold 'rise' for now, because the tense fix settles it.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourist visiting the museum rise.

moves.say: Next, the tense. '2010' is a past year, so 'rise' must change to 'rose'. I change only that word.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourist visiting the museum rose.

moves.say: Comma splice: I look for two full sentences joined by a comma. This sentence has only one clause, so there is nothing to fix.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourist visiting the museum rose.

moves.say: There is or there are: I look for these words. The sentence has none, so I move on without changes.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourist visiting the museum rose.

moves.say: Now the plural. 'The number of' is followed by a plural noun, because many tourists are counted, so 'tourist' needs an -s.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourists visiting the museum rose.

moves.say: I copy 'museum' and 'tourist' from the question letter by letter. Both are spelled correctly, so I change nothing.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourists visiting the museum rose.

moves.say: Use 'the number of' for countable things. Tourists are countable, so the phrase is correct and stays.
moves.build: In 2010 the number of tourists visiting the museum rose.

demo.answer: In 2010 the number of tourists visiting the museum rose.

band8.band8: Knows own three most common errors and checks for each one by name in the final minutes.

band8.typical: Uses only simple sentences to stay safe, or complex ones that break down halfway.
band8.band8: Builds complex sentences from sentences already correct, adding one clause at a time and checking it before moving on.

band8.typical: Writes long sentences joined by commas, which blurs where one idea ends.
band8.band8: Splits comma-joined sentences into two, or joins them with a proper conjunction, so every sentence has a clear edge.

band8.typical: Uses a word without checking its form, such as "informations" or "an advice".
band8.band8: Checks uncountable nouns and word forms in the final scan, because a correct simple word beats a wrong advanced one.

band8.typical: Corrects grammar but leaves a sentence that does not answer the question.
band8.band8: Checks while correcting that every sentence still supports the position or the overview, and cuts any that do not.

title: Task 1: Bar chart and line graph
what: You look at a chart and write a report of at least 150 words. The examiner is not asking you to copy every number. They want you to pick the key features and compare them. An 'overview' is two sentences that give the big picture without numbers, and it is required.

steps.do: Read the title, axes and units. Note what is measured, the three foods, the country and the years.
steps.why: These decide your paraphrase and your past tense. Wrong units are a common mistake.

steps.do: Pick the key features: each line's start, its peak or low, and the point where two lines cross.
steps.why: Only the main features belong in the report. Describe the data alone, with no opinions or reasons for the trends.

steps.do: Group the lines: those that rose go in body paragraph one, and the line that fell goes in body paragraph two.
steps.why: Grouping gives two clear comparisons, rising against falling, rather than a list of lines.

steps.do: Write the introduction: one sentence that paraphrases the title, naming the measure, the foods, the country and the years.
steps.why: One paraphrase sentence shows you understood the graph, without adding facts or reasons.

steps.do: Write the overview in two sentences: the general trend of each group, then the cross-over. No numbers.
steps.why: The overview is required and gives the big picture. Numbers belong in the body paragraphs.

steps.do: Write body paragraph one: the rising lines, hamburgers and pizza, with their starting figures, growth and peak.
steps.why: The rising lines form one group, so the reader gets one clear trend supported by a few key figures.

steps.do: Write body paragraph two: the falling line, fish and chips, with its starting figure, dip and final low.
steps.why: The falling line gets its own paragraph, so the decline is set clearly against the rises.

steps.do: Check units, years and verbs. Make sure each number matches the chart.
steps.why: Accuracy is part of the task. A wrong number or tense costs marks.

tricks: Use different verbs for change: rose, climbed, fell, dropped, peaked at, levelled off. Do not repeat 'increased' four times.
Compare in one sentence instead of two. 'Cars rose to 40% whereas buses fell to 10%' shows comparison and saves words.
Use approximation words for numbers: about, roughly, just over, nearly. They are safe when the chart is not exact.
For a line graph, always include the start point, the end point and the highest or lowest point of each key line.
traps: Describing every number. Select the key features and leave the small details out.
Giving reasons or opinions. Say what the chart shows, not why it happened, because you can only use the data.
Putting numbers in the overview. Keep it general, and give numbers in the body paragraphs.
Mixing tenses. If the dates are all in the past, use the past tense for the whole report.
checklist: Does my overview have no numbers, and show the main trend?
Did I choose two or three key features, not every figure?
Did I group the data and compare, not describe left to right?
Are my units, dates and tenses right?

frames.name: Introduction
lines: The [bar chart / line graph] [shows / compares / illustrates] [what is measured] in [place] [over the period / in year].
The [chart / graph] gives information about [topic] between [year] and [year].
[Measure] in [place] is presented in the [bar chart / line graph] for [period].

frames.name: Overview
lines: Overall, [item A] [rose / fell] over the period, while [item B] [stayed stable / moved in the opposite direction].
It is clear that [item A] was [the highest / the most popular] at every point, whereas [item B] was [the lowest].
The most noticeable feature is that [item A] [changed in this way], unlike [item B].

frames.name: Rise, fall, peak and gap
lines: [Item] [rose / fell] from [number] in [year] to [number] in [year].
[Item] [peaked / bottomed out] at [number] in [year] before [falling / recovering] to [number].
The gap between [item A] and [item B] [widened / narrowed] from [number] to [number].

example.prompt: Write one sentence about the rise in cycling from 2005 to 2015, from a line graph.
example.weak: Cycling went up a lot from 2005 to 2015.
example.strong: The number of people who cycled to work rose steadily from about 20% in 2005 to just over 35% in 2015.
example.why: The strong sentence names exactly what is measured, uses a precise verb and adverb, and gives approximate figures with the years.

demo.prompt: The line graph shows changes in the consumption of three types of fast food in the United Kingdom between 1970 and 1990.

moves.say: I read the prompt: three fast foods in the UK, measured as consumption from 1970 to 1990. The past tense fits the whole report.
I pick the key features: hamburgers and pizza rise, hamburgers reach 500 grams, fish and chips fall, and the lines cross by 1985.
I group the data: the two rising lines go in body paragraph one, and the falling line goes in body paragraph two.
Introduction, paraphrase: I restate the title in my own words, with the measure, the foods, the country and the years.
moves.build: The line graph illustrates changes in the consumption levels of three different types of fast food in the United Kingdom between 1970 and 1990.

moves.say: Overview, general trend: I say that two foods rose and one fell, with no figures.
moves.build: The line graph illustrates changes in the consumption levels of three different types of fast food in the United Kingdom between 1970 and 1990. Overall, it is clear that while the consumption of hamburgers and pizza experienced a marked upward trajectory throughout the period, fish and chips followed a significant downward trend.

moves.say: Overview, cross-over: I say that hamburgers started lowest but became the most consumed food by the end.
moves.build: The line graph illustrates changes in the consumption levels of three different types of fast food in the United Kingdom between 1970 and 1990. Overall, it is clear that while the consumption of hamburgers and pizza experienced a marked upward trajectory throughout the period, fish and chips followed a significant downward trend. Additionally, despite starting as by far the least favoured item, hamburgers overtook fish and chips to become the most consumed food by the final year.

what: You get one or more pie charts, each showing parts of a whole, usually as percentages. You write a report of at least 150 words. The skill is comparing the slices, inside one pie and between two pies. The overview must name the biggest slice and, if there are two pies, the biggest change.

steps.do: Read the title and note what the whole pie stands for, such as total household spending, and the year of each pie.
steps.why: The pie is 100% of something. Your introduction must say what that something is.

steps.do: Rank the slices in each pie from largest to smallest. Mark the largest and the smallest.
steps.why: Ranking shows you what to compare. The biggest and smallest are almost always key features.

steps.do: If there are two pies, find the slices that changed most between them. Note which grew and which shrank.
steps.why: The biggest change is the main story of two pies, and it belongs in your overview.

steps.do: Write the introduction: one sentence that paraphrases the title, saying what the pies show and when.
steps.why: One paraphrase sentence proves you understand the chart, without adding new facts or reasons.

steps.do: Write the overview in two sentences: the largest slice, then the biggest change. No numbers.
steps.why: The overview is required. It names the main points for two pies and states facts only, with no reasons.

steps.do: Write body paragraph one: the largest slices, housing and other costs, with their figures in both years.
steps.why: The largest slices come first, so the report opens with the biggest shares and their changes.

steps.do: Write body paragraph two: food and transport, the slices that shrank, with their figures and how they compare.
steps.why: The smaller slices get their own paragraph, so each comparison is clear and the figures easy to check.

steps.do: Check that the percentages you quote add up sensibly, and that each slice is matched to the right label.
steps.why: Swapping two labels is an easy mistake and it changes the whole meaning.

tricks: Vary the way you give numbers: 40%, two fifths, 'the largest share', 'a quarter', 'just under half'. It shows range.
Use 'accounted for', 'made up' and 'represented' to say what a slice is: 'Rent accounted for 30% of spending.'
Group small slices together. 'The other three categories each made up less than 10%' saves time.
For two pies, compare the same slice in both pies in one sentence. It is the clearest kind of comparison.
traps: Reading the slices one by one clockwise. This is a list, not a report. Rank and compare instead.
Using 'number' for percentages. A pie shows shares, so write 'the proportion' or 'the percentage', not 'the number of'.
Saying the slices 'increased' in a single pie. A single pie has no change over time, so say 'was larger than'.
Giving a reason, such as why people spend more on food. You can only report what the chart shows.

title: Task 1: Process diagrams
what: A process diagram shows the stages of how something is made or how something happens in nature. You write at least 150 words describing the stages in order. Use the passive, because the machine or the natural force matters more than a person. The overview counts the stages and says where the process starts and ends.

steps.do: Decide whether the process is a line (a start and an end) or a cycle (it goes round and round).
steps.why: A line and a cycle need different overviews. This process is a line, from raw fruit to packaged oil.

steps.do: Count and number the stages. Note the input, the action and the result at each stage.
steps.why: Missing a stage is an error. Counting helps you not to forget one, and the count goes in the overview.

steps.do: Split the stages into two halves: the first half goes in body paragraph one, the second in body paragraph two.
steps.why: Two halves give two balanced paragraphs, each covering a clear part of the process in order.

steps.do: Write the introduction: one sentence that paraphrases the title, saying what the diagram shows and its stages.
steps.why: One paraphrase sentence shows you understood the diagram, without adding facts or reasons.

steps.do: Write the overview in two sentences: the number of stages with the start and end, then the key method. No details.
steps.why: The overview is required. It gives the big picture, and it states facts only, with no reasons or opinions.

steps.do: Write body paragraph one: the first half of the stages, from harvesting to malaxation, in passive sequence.
steps.why: Sequencers and the passive keep the order clear, and each stage in the first half is described once.

steps.do: Write body paragraph two: the second half of the stages, from centrifuge to packaging, in passive sequence.
steps.why: The second half gets its own paragraph, so the reader follows the rest of the process in order.

steps.do: Check that every stage appears once, in the right order, with the right equipment named.
steps.why: The order is the whole point. Two stages in the wrong order change the process.

tricks: Use the present simple passive: 'The paper is heated', 'The mixture is filtered'. Process diagrams use the present tense.
Link stages with sequencers: first, next, after that, then, subsequently, finally. Do not use 'then' every time.
Join two short stages with 'which' or 'before': 'The sheet is dried before it is cut into reels.'
For a cycle, say 'the cycle begins with' and end with 'the cycle then repeats'.
traps: Giving opinions, such as saying a stage is important or bad. A process report is only description.
Using 'I' or 'you'. Use the passive voice instead, such as 'the water is boiled'.
Copying the labels exactly from the diagram for every stage. Change the wording where you can.
Putting too much detail in the overview. Keep it to the number of stages, the start, the end and the key method.

title: Task 2: Opinion essay ("To what extent do you agree?")
what: You are given a statement and asked how far you agree. Task 2 needs at least 250 words and is worth more than Task 1. The examiner wants one clear position, which means your own side, kept the same from start to finish.

steps.do: Read the statement slowly and underline the key words. Circle any limiting word such as 'all' or 'only'.
steps.why: Answering a slightly different statement is the most common way to lose marks.

steps.do: Choose your position: agree, disagree or partly agree. Make it your final choice before you write.
steps.why: A clear position is required. Changing your mind halfway makes the essay confusing.

steps.do: Write the introduction: paraphrase the statement, then give a clear thesis: your position and two reasons.
steps.why: Two sentences do the job: the paraphrase shows you understood the statement, and the thesis shows your position.

steps.do: Write body paragraph one: reason one as a topic sentence, then an explanation, an example and a result sentence that links back.
steps.why: The topic sentence shows the point at once, and the result sentence ties the paragraph back to your position.

steps.do: Write body paragraph two: reason two as a topic sentence, then an explanation, an example and a result sentence that links back.
steps.why: Each paragraph develops one reason, so the second needs its own topic sentence, example and closing result.

steps.do: Write the conclusion in two sentences: restate your position and main reasons, then give one final takeaway.
steps.why: The restatement closes the argument, and the final takeaway ends firmly without introducing a new idea.

steps.do: Check the word count and your position. Make sure the introduction and conclusion agree.
steps.why: If the two disagree, the examiner cannot tell what you really think.

tricks: Say your position in the same words in the introduction and conclusion, for example 'I strongly agree' or 'I partly agree'.
Use opinion phrases: 'In my view', 'I firmly believe that', 'I would argue that'.
Plan for 5 minutes. Write the position, two reasons and two examples before you start the first sentence.
Relevant example: give one short, real-world example in a single sentence, such as 'In Finland, for instance, ...'. Keep it specific and true.
traps: Sitting on the fence. If you partly agree, say exactly which part you accept and which part you reject.
Writing about the topic in general instead of the statement. Use the key words from the question.
Using a memorised essay that ignores the question. Examiners spot it at once, so answer the exact question you are given.
Adding a new idea in the conclusion. Only repeat your main points there.
Writing fewer than 250 words. A short essay loses marks, so practise until 260 to 290 words feels normal.

Using informal words such as 'kids'. Write 'children'. 'A lot of' is fine in speech, but in an essay prefer 'many' or 'a large number of' with countable nouns, and 'a great deal of' or 'much' with uncountable nouns.

steps.do: List the causes first, then write solutions that answer them. Each solution should fix one of the causes you listed.

steps.do: Choose one example for each cause and each solution. A short real-world example is enough.

steps.do: Write the introduction in two sentences: paraphrase the problem, then name the main causes and the main solutions.

steps.why: A missing part or a solution that answers no cause is the most common reason for a low score here.

title: Task 2: Two-part question essay
what: You are given two separate questions about one topic, and you must answer both. Task 2 needs at least 250 words. The examiner checks that both questions are answered fully, so a missing answer is the biggest risk.

steps.do: Underline each question. Number them 1 and 2 on your paper.
steps.why: It is easy to answer one question well and forget the other.

steps.do: Write a short, direct answer to each question. These answers go into the introduction thesis, so each must be clear.
steps.why: A direct answer to each part earns marks, and the thesis shows the examiner both answers early.

steps.do: Add one reason and one example for each answer.
steps.why: Each part needs support to feel developed, not just stated.

steps.do: Write the introduction in two sentences: paraphrase the topic, then answer both questions directly in the thesis.
steps.why: The paraphrase shows you understood the topic, and the thesis answers both questions before the body starts.

steps.do: Write body paragraph one to answer question 1: topic sentence, explanation, example, then a result sentence.
steps.why: One paragraph per question keeps the answers separate and easy to mark.

steps.do: Write body paragraph two to answer question 2: signposted topic sentence, explanation, example, then a result sentence.
steps.why: The signpost guides the reader to the new part, and the result sentence answers it clearly.

steps.do: Write the conclusion in two sentences: restate both answers, then give one final thought.
steps.why: Restating both answers proves each part was answered, and the final thought ends firmly without a new idea.

steps.do: Check that question 1 has body one, question 2 has body two, and the introduction answers both directly.
steps.why: Answering only one question, or only saying you will answer both, is the biggest risk here.

tricks: Use the words of each question in your topic sentence, so the examiner sees which part you are answering.
Use signposting: 'Turning to the question of', 'As for the second question'.
Answer in order. Question 1 first and question 2 second.
Relevant example: give one short, real-world example in a single sentence, such as 'In Finland, for instance, ...'. Keep it specific and true.
traps: Answering only one question. Number the questions and tick them off.
Mixing both answers in one paragraph. Give each question its own paragraph.
Using a memorised essay that ignores the question. Examiners spot it at once, so answer the exact question you are given.
Adding a new idea in the conclusion. Only repeat your main points there.
Writing fewer than 250 words. A short essay loses marks, so practise until 260 to 290 words feels normal.

Using informal words such as 'kids'. Write 'children'. 'A lot of' is fine in speech, but in an essay prefer 'many' or 'a large number of' with countable nouns, and 'a great deal of' or 'much' with uncountable nouns.
checklist: Did I answer both questions directly in the introduction?
Does each question have its own body paragraph?
Does each body paragraph have a topic sentence, a reason, an example and a result sentence?
Is my conclusion free of new ideas?

title: Task 2: Advantages and disadvantages essay
what: You are given a change or trend and asked whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. 'Outweigh' means 'are greater than'. Task 2 needs at least 250 words. The examiner wants you to choose a side and weigh both sides.

steps.do: Read the question. Check whether it asks you to list both sides or to say which side is greater.
steps.why: The wording decides your plan, so do not skip it.

steps.do: List two advantages and two disadvantages. Add a short example to each.
steps.why: Having ideas on both sides lets you compare them fairly.

steps.do: Decide which side is stronger. Plan the weaker side for body one, kept brief, and the stronger side for body two, expanded.
steps.why: The weaker side is bounded so the stronger side carries the argument, and the essay ends on your strongest point.

steps.do: Write the introduction in two sentences: paraphrase the trend, then state which side is greater and why.
steps.why: The paraphrase shows you understood the trend, and the position sentence gives your verdict early.

steps.do: Write body one on the weaker side, kept brief: topic sentence, explanation, example, then a result sentence that concedes its force.
steps.why: Acknowledging this side fairly shows balance, but keeping it short stops it outweighing your argument.

steps.do: Write body two on the stronger side, expanded: topic sentence with 'On the other hand', explanation, second point, then a result sentence weighing the sides.
steps.why: This is the weighing step. The longer paragraph and its comparison show why one side is greater.

steps.do: Write the conclusion in two sentences: evaluate the sides and repeat your verdict, then give your recommendation.
steps.why: The evaluation confirms your answer, and the recommendation ends firmly without adding a new idea.

steps.do: Check that the weaker side is in body one, the stronger side in body two, and your verdict matches the introduction.
steps.why: A reversed order or a changed verdict makes the argument look unplanned and weakens your answer.

tricks: Use weighing words: 'Although', 'Despite this', 'Nevertheless', 'on balance'. They show you are comparing.
Say how big each point is: 'a minor drawback', 'a major benefit'.
Put the weaker side in body one and the stronger side in body two, so the essay ends on your strongest point.
Relevant example: give one short, real-world example in a single sentence, such as 'In Finland, for instance, ...'. Keep it specific and true.
traps: Listing advantages and disadvantages with no decision. Say which side is greater and why.
Giving the weaker side more space than the stronger one. Keep it brief and bounded, and expand the stronger side.
Using a memorised essay that ignores the question. Examiners spot it at once, so answer the exact question you are given.
Adding a new idea in the conclusion. Only repeat your main points there.
Writing fewer than 250 words. A short essay loses marks, so practise until 260 to 290 words feels normal.

Using informal words such as 'kids'. Write 'children'. 'A lot of' is fine in speech, but in an essay prefer 'many' or 'a large number of' with countable nouns, and 'a great deal of' or 'much' with uncountable nouns.
checklist: Did I choose a side in the introduction and conclusion?
Did I use weighing words to compare the two sides?
Is the weaker side in body one and the stronger side in body two?
Does each body paragraph end with a result sentence?
Is my conclusion free of new ideas?
